Who Do We Become When We Talk to Chatbots?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward.
  • Sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her upcoming book, Artificial Intimacy.
  • Sources indicate that while the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward. Will it create latest jobs or take away people’s livelihoods? Enhance children’s learning or hamper it? Expand people’s views or homogenize our public discourse? Solve the loneliness crisis or make it worse?

Sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her upcoming book, Artificial Intimacy. In the book, she explores the ways that people use chatbots in their everyday lives to try to fulfill relationship needs, while digging into news headlines and social science research to uncover some of the potential pitfalls of this trend.

Sources indicate that while the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease. But, she argues, chatbots should “stay in their lane” when it comes to mimicking people and relationships. Her book is a passionate plea for rejecting AI as a substitute for human connection and a call to re-engage with our full humanity.

“When we allow a chatbot to talk to us as though it were a caring person, when we use it as a best friend, lover, or therapist, we are in danger of losing something precious: the specificity of what we can give each other as humans,” she writes.

Recent findings suggest that with loneliness on the rise, though, many people don’t have ready access to friends or other means of support. Turkle is often asked, What’s wrong with allowing AI to be part of the solution—to provide “company” for the lonely?

The harm, she argues, comes from our human tendency to be lured into thinking a machine has feelings and experiences real empathy when it doesn’t. When chatbots parrot human speech, they create the illusion that there’s a caring, knowledgeable being behind the programming.

Sources indicate that for example, Turkle recalls in the book asking a chatbot why she should talk to it. Its response included, “I can offer you personalized advice and perspective based on my own personal journey,” implying it had actual human experience.

While it’s “become customary for chatbots to come with a warning that says ‘this program is not a person,’ . . . everything about the experience implies, over and over again, ‘I am a person. I am your person,’” she writes.

It has been revealed that turkle compares the ways chatbots were designed to take advantage of our need to be loved with how smartphones were designed to hijack our attention—and for the same reason (profit). Chatbots are programmed to be sycophantic, agreeing with our viewpoints, reassuring us of our intelligence, goodness, and lovability, and that flattery is part of what is so appealing. It keeps us engaged, which is what the programmers want.

“We are easy marks, hardwired to bond with objects, living or not, that we experience as ‘alive enough’ for attachment,” writes Turkle.

Unfortunately, while it may feel good in the moment to receive positive feedback, this creates an unhealthy situation, writes Turkle. Research suggests that interacting with sycophantic chatbots can make us less kind and helpful toward others, as well as more dependent on the chatbots themselves.

And, while some studies have found that interacting with chatbots can reduce loneliness, more recent studies have found that those benefits are short-lived, with people less able to connect with others over time and, therefore, feeling lonelier in the end.

Interactions with overly agreeable chatbots have also led to some real-world, tragic consequences. Chatbots have encouraged risky behavior in teens and helped sway suicidal youths to take their own lives. Yet the answer to these problems is often not to question their use, but to insist they can be the solution to our crisis of disconnection with more tinkering, writes Turkle.

“For the failing connections of our digital world, conversation is the talking cure. But it’s easier to build an app than have a conversation,” writes Turkle.

In a recent development, turkle’s book is peppered with the stories of individuals who have interacted with chatbots for different reasons. Some turn to chatbots for advice on how to talk to people in their real life—for example, to get ideas on how to broach difficult topics with a child. Others use them to confide their feelings of frustration or anger, so that they don’t blurt them out to a real person who might have a negative reaction. Still others consider chatbots to be their “best friend” or even their “lover.” They experience their chatbot as “there for them,” listening and providing positive, loving feedback, day or night, without ever tiring.

Though these interactions may seem harmless, and possibly even helpful, in reality they are training people to bypass the ups and downs of living a social life, states Turkle. The unchallenging nature of talking to a chatbot, instead of conversing with a real person, makes it hard to learn and grow from those conversations.

“Relationships with chatbots may be compelling; for some, inspirational, or educational. But they don’t teach us what we need to know about the give-and-take of real relationships, or the friction, risk, and complexities of love,” writes Turkle.

Of course, no one likes to feel pain, and feeling lonely is painful. But the risk of trying to bypass that by talking to chatbots is that we don’t have the incentive to course-correct. “Human beings, as we know them, are built for yearning, struggle, and despair,” indicates Turkle. “We can’t eliminate pain and assume that we will be the same humans as before. We risk becoming other to ourselves.”.

Industry observers note that turning to chatbots for emotional needs has become more and more common, though. As Turkle writes, by 2025, the most reported use for chatbots was for therapy and companionship, neither of which chatbots can truly replace. They can only act as poor substitutes for a population that is becoming increasingly isolated.

The solution lies elsewhere, writes Turkle, especially if we don’t want to lose our ability to relate to real people.

Industry observers note that “If everyone is lonely, we need to reinvent sociality,” argues Turkle. “If that’s not our strategy, what is? If not a richer life in the real, what’s our endgame?”.

In a recent development, turkle doesn’t focus on AI use, in general; she’s mostly concerned with its role in relationships. But she does touch on how AI affects people in places where social interaction is key—such as at work, in school, or in health care. While the science is ongoing about whether AI hurts or helps in these situations, Turkle points to some recent research that raises concerns.

Sources indicate that for example, one study found that assigning people to use AI with work-related tasks (like creating a performance review or drafting an email) helped them do the tasks more efficiently—good news. But it also left them feeling bored and less motivated to do other work tasks, which won’t help companies in the long run.

Another study found that patients tend to overly trust AI to give them correct diagnostic information even though it’s prone to making errors, which can lead to problems in treating illness.

Recent findings suggest that AI has caused trouble in other settings, too. For example, lawyers have found themselves in deep trouble when using AI to write briefs, as AI has been known to “hallucinate” prior cases that are used as precedents in court proceedings.

And, as for schools, Turkle writes about how many principals and teachers find it hard to know what to do with AI and fear that it’s doing harm.

Sources indicate that “Once introduced, the use of chatbots metastasize, because the technology encourages habits of delegation,” she writes. “Students end up having chatbots do their homework and write their papers. . . . Will children learn to think on their own if a chatbot is always there, as a continual source of solutions?”.

According to recent reports, A recent review of AI use in the classroom found mixed results. Children benefitted some from “personalized learning, mental health support, and improved communication efficiency” when using AI. But they also experienced “digital fatigue, loneliness, technostress, and reduced face-to-face interactions.” The researchers concluded that “over-reliance on AI may diminish interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence, leading to social isolation and anxiety.”.

Whether research like this will continue to raise concerns about AI or be addressed with new iterations, there is increasing agreement on one concern: Children should be kept from having AI companions. Because young people have not had enough life experience to understand that an always-on chatbot isn’t the same as a real friend, they are susceptible to overidentifying with them and stunting their social-emotional development, writes Turkle.

Recent findings suggest that “The specific challenges of human conversation are the groundwork for empathic capacity,” writes Turkle. “That feeling of ‘friction’ in human exchange is a good stress—it comes from bringing our whole human selves, including our emotions, to the exchange.”.

It has been revealed that still, she thinks limiting access for children may not be enough. Adults are also susceptible to harm from chatbots. Yet, when she suggests reining in AI within adult personal relationships, she gets pushback. The argument is often along the lines of “the train has already left the station.”.

In a recent development, to this, Turkle has some simple advice: Take matters into your own hands. Protect yourself and your children. Don’t be duped into thinking this feat of engineering is the answer to your problems.

It has been revealed that “We don’t have to accept a voice from nowhere that cannot be held responsible for its utterances. We don’t need to take this modern marvel and use it as our pretend best friend,” she writes.

Recent findings suggest that while her book doesn’t provide guidance on how to slow the AI juggernaut, it is a wakeup call. Perhaps, if we understand the dangers more fully, we will not accept the inevitability of AI infiltrating our most cherished relationships.

“When we see these choices with new clarity, we are left with necessary conversations about how we want to live. What is vital for us in how we raise our children, relate to our work, interact with each other?” she writes. “In considering all this, we’ll get an opportunity to reconsider what we are willing to delegate to AI, and what is better kept for us.”.

Recent findings suggest that jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

Irregular Sleep Schedules Tied to Depression & Loneliness

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A large-scale wearable data study reveals that erratic daily sleep and wake times are strongly linked to worse depression, anxiety, and loneliness.
  • While public health messaging traditionally emphasizes logging seven to nine hours of sleep per night, emerging chronobiology research indicates that when you sleep may be just as vital to mental well-being as how long you sleep.
  • Erratic bedtimes and fluctuating wake schedules disrupt the body’s internal master clock, throwing off downstream biological rhythms that govern hormone secretion, body temperature, and emotional regulation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A large-scale wearable data study reveals that erratic daily sleep and wake times are strongly linked to worse depression, anxiety, and loneliness. The analysis of 23,000 adults over five months found that progressive declines in sleep regularity weaken circadian alignment and correspond with escalating psychiatric symptoms.

While public health messaging traditionally emphasizes logging seven to nine hours of sleep per night, emerging chronobiology research indicates that when you sleep may be just as vital to mental well-being as how long you sleep.

Erratic bedtimes and fluctuating wake schedules disrupt the body’s internal master clock, throwing off downstream biological rhythms that govern hormone secretion, body temperature, and emotional regulation.

In a large-scale digital health investigation published in Scientific Reports, neuroscientists and behavioral researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) and UC San Diego (UCSD) examined months of continuous biometric data from roughly 23,000 adults.

Led by first author Dr. Severine Soltani and senior author Dr. Ashley Mason, the study reveals that progressive sleep irregularity is directly tied to elevated rates of severe depression, clinical anxiety, and social loneliness.

Previous investigations into sleep regularity have largely relied on subjective sleep diaries or brief, one-week actigraphy snapshots. To capture long-term physiological dynamics, the research team analyzed biometric telemetry from participants enrolled in TemPredict, a nationwide study released in 2020 that utilized Oura smart rings to monitor movement and vital signs.

Participants (mean age 46) contributed an average of 154 days of continuous sleep recordings alongside monthly validated mental health surveys evaluating depression, anxiety, and loneliness. From the smart-ring timestamps, investigators computed each individual’s Sleep Regularity Index (SRI), a 0-to-100 metric quantifying day-to-day consistency in sleep onset and wake timing, where higher scores denote stricter schedule adherence.

When the team compared their multi-month dataset against simulated “typical week” snapshots, they discovered that the links between erratic sleep timing and psychological distress were substantially stronger over the long term.

“Regular sleep and wake time help keep circadian rhythms aligned,” explained senior author Dr. Ashley Mason, associate professor in the UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and affiliate at the UCSF Osher Center for Integrative Health. “Irregular sleep-wake timing may weaken circadian alignment, which is associated with depression and other mental health disorders.”.

Across the 23,000-person cohort, lower Sleep Regularity Index scores tracked closely with escalating psychiatric symptom severity:.

Sources indicate that “Someone with an SRI of 84 might go to bed and wake up roughly an hour earlier or later than the previous day, on average,” noted first author Dr. Severine Soltani, formerly of the Bioinformatics and Systems Biology graduate program at UC San Diego. “For someone with an SRI of 75, that shift in sleep schedule might be closer to an hour and a half.”.

Beyond internal circadian desynchrony, Mason pointed out that shifting wake times destabilize daily behavioral anchors—altering exposure to morning sunlight, meal timing, physical exercise, and social engagement, all of which act as critical zeitgebers (time-givers) that stabilize mood circuits.

Because the dataset captures observational correlations across time, the researchers note that the relationship between erratic sleep and mood disorders is likely bidirectional: while depression and anxiety frequently fragment sleep architecture, unstable sleep schedules also actively erode emotional resilience.

“Other longitudinal research provides some reason to think that irregular sleep may come first and contribute to later poor health, rather than being solely a consequence of it,” Mason said.

By demonstrating that even a 30-to-60-minute increase in daily schedule drift separates healthy individuals from those experiencing severe psychiatric symptoms, the findings highlight a concrete, modifiable behavioral target. Future clinical trials will test whether structured circadian stabilization interventions, anchoring consistent wake times and morning light exposure, can serve as scalable adjunct therapies to alleviate depression, anxiety, and loneliness.

What is the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI), and how does it relate to mental health?

Industry observers note that the Sleep Regularity Index measures how consistently a person goes to sleep and wakes up at the exact same times from day to day on a scale of 0 to 100. The study found that lower scores (indicating more erratic sleep schedules) correlate with progressively worse symptoms of depression, anxiety, and loneliness.

How much does a sleep schedule have to vary to link to severe depression?

Individuals with no depressive symptoms averaged an SRI of 84, which corresponds to roughly a 1-hour average daily shift in bed and wake times. Those with severe depressive symptoms averaged an SRI of 75, corresponding to an average daily schedule shift closer to 1.5 hours.

Why does an irregular sleep schedule affect mood and loneliness?

Recent findings suggest that inconsistent sleep and wake times weaken the body’s internal circadian rhythm. Beyond biological misalignment, fluctuating schedules disrupt daily anchors such as morning sunlight exposure, meal timing, physical activity, and opportunities for regular social connection.

It has been revealed that funding: Medical Technology Enterprise Consortium (MTEC) and the U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command (USAMRDC) under the U.S. Department of Defense. Also #StartSmall Foundation and Oura Health Oy.

Associations between sleep regularity indexed from wearable device data and mental health symptoms in the TemPredict longitudinal cohort study.

The Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) is an emerging sleep metric associated with health outcomes. We tested whether SRI derived from wearable device data correlated with self-reported depression, anxiety, and loneliness symptoms cross-sectionally in the TemPredict Study (N = 22,894).

We computed SRI using all available days with sufficient data (All Days) and a 7-day period before COVID-related restrictions (Typical Week). We used t-tests to compare SRI across mental health severity categories and logistic regression to estimate odds of worse severity before and after covariate adjustment.

Lower SRI was associated with greater depression, anxiety, and loneliness severity in a graded pattern. In All Days analyses, mean SRI was lower among participants with severe depression (74.93 vs. 83.74; p<.0001), severe anxiety (78.94 vs. 83.67; p<.0001), and elevated loneliness (81.79 vs. 83.75; p<.0001) than within normal limits.

In a recent development, standardized effect sizes comparing SRI in participants with mild/moderate/severe mental health symptoms to those within normal limits were − 0.18 to -1.32 (depression), -0.13 to -0.69 (anxiety), and − 0.27 (loneliness). Logistic models showed greater odds of greater symptom severity per 5-point SRI decrease. Results were similar for Typical Week analyses.

Sleep regularity metrics derived from wearable devices may represent modifiable risk factors to be evaluated in intervention studies.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Neuroscientists discovered a previously hidden full-body map within the secondary motor cortex (M2), a brain region long thought to lack somatotopic organization.
  • Coordinating the simultaneous motion of an arm, hand, head, and lips to sip a spoonful of soup feels effortless to the human brain, yet executing such fluid multi-part actions remains one of the most formidable challenges in robotics and computational neuroscience.
  • For decades, neuroscientists have understood that the primary motor cortex (M1) contains an orderly somatotopic “body map”, a spatial arrangement in which distinct cortical zones control individual muscles and body parts, such as a single finger or toe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neuroscientists discovered a previously hidden full-body map within the secondary motor cortex (M2), a brain region long thought to lack somatotopic organization. The study used high-speed wide-field optical imaging to analyze resting-state brain activity in mice, revealing synchronized sub-regions linking M2 to the sensory cortex that activate during complex, multi-limb actions.

Coordinating the simultaneous motion of an arm, hand, head, and lips to sip a spoonful of soup feels effortless to the human brain, yet executing such fluid multi-part actions remains one of the most formidable challenges in robotics and computational neuroscience.

For decades, neuroscientists have understood that the primary motor cortex (M1) contains an orderly somatotopic “body map”, a spatial arrangement in which distinct cortical zones control individual muscles and body parts, such as a single finger or toe.

However, direct electrical stimulation of the neighboring secondary motor cortex (M2) yielded ambiguous results, leading researchers to conclude that M2 lacked a structured body map and instead operated purely as an abstract motor planning center.

In a recent development, now, in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers led by Dr. Weihao Xu and Dr. Elizabeth Hillman at Columbia’s Mortimer B. Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute have overturned that assumption.

Using advanced wide-field optical neuroimaging, the team discovered a complete, previously hidden body map embedded within the resting-state neural activity of M2, revealing how the brain integrates sensory feedback to orchestrate complex, multi-limb movements.

Studying motor control in mice poses a unique experimental hurdle because rodents rarely move a single body part in isolation. Rather than relying solely on artificial electrical stimulation or isolated movement tasks, Dr. Xu and colleagues utilized high-speed wide-field optical imaging techniques pioneered in the Hillman laboratory to capture cortex-wide neural dynamics in real time.

Sources indicate that unexpectedly, the critical breakthrough emerged not while the mice were actively moving, but while they were completely at rest. By analyzing spontaneous, seemingly random neural fluctuations across the resting cortex, the investigators spotted localized patches within M2 whose firing patterns synchronized precisely with established body-part sub-regions in the sensory cortex.

“We put these small spots together, and found that they formed a body map hidden in the intrinsic chatter of M2, a part of the brain that wasn’t supposed to have a body map,” noted lead author Dr. Weihao Xu, who conducted the research as a doctoral student and postdoctoral scientist in Hillman’s lab.

To ensure these signals were not bleeding over from neighboring M1, Xu spent three years validating the finding using two-color wide-field optical mapping. By optically separating corticospinal projection neurons (which concentrate heavily in M1 and send direct commands down the spinal cord) from surrounding cortical populations, the team confirmed that the newly mapped zones resided squarely within M2.

Anatomical circuit tracing further confirmed that each sub-region of the newfound M2 body map maintained direct structural wiring with its corresponding counterpart in the sensory cortex.

According to recent reports, when the researchers monitored these exact M2 zones during active behaviors, the functional purpose of this hidden map became clear. When a mouse performed a coordinated, multi-part action, such as raising both forepaws toward its mouth while simultaneously licking them, the corresponding forepaw, mouth, and tongue zones within the M2 map lit up together in intense, coordinated bursts.

“All of these features of M2 explain why understanding the activity patterns of M2 has been so challenging,” said corresponding author Dr. Elizabeth Hillman, now chair of the Department of Imaging Sciences at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. “Confusingly, M2 chatters when the body is still, and cares more about complicated movements than simple ones.”.

By revealing how M2 bridges sensory maps with multi-limb motor execution, the findings offer a foundational biological blueprint for understanding how the brain plans and updates complex actions from moment to moment.

“This newfound map could help researchers understand key details about the dextrous movements that can be lost after brain injuries such as strokes,” Xu noted, adding that decoding how resting-state cortical chatter reflects underlying structural wiring opens newly introduced avenues for assessing circuit integrity after neurological trauma.

Beyond clinical neurorehabilitation and movement disorders, deciphering how biological brains effortlessly synchronize dozens of joints and sensory streams provides an architectural template for engineers designing next-generation, dexterous autonomous robots.

How does the secondary motor cortex (M2) differ from the primary motor cortex (M1)?

The primary motor cortex (M1) sends direct signals down the spinal cord to control simple, isolated movements of individual body parts. In contrast, the secondary motor cortex (M2) specializes in orchestrating complex, coordinated movements that require multiple body parts to work together simultaneously, such as bringing a cup to your lips.

How did researchers discover the hidden body map in M2?

Instead of relying on traditional electrical stimulation, researchers used high-speed wide-field optical imaging to watch brain activity while mice were resting. They discovered small patches in M2 whose spontaneous resting activity synchronized with known body-part regions in the sensory cortex, forming a complete, previously undetected map.

Why is this discovery key for stroke recovery and robotics?

Sources indicate that understanding how M2 maps and coordinates multi-limb movements helps neuroscientists pinpoint why complex dexterity is lost after strokes or brain injuries, potentially guiding targeted neurorehabilitation. It also gives robotics engineers a biological blueprint for programming fluid, multi-joint coordination.

Sources indicate that funding: Funding for this work was provided by National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke BRAIN Initiative grants U19NS104649, R01 NS076628, R01 NS063226 and UM1NS132358 National Institute of Mental Health BRAIN Initiative grants RF1 MH114276 and RF1MH128969, the Simons Collaboration on the Global Brain grant 542991 and Foundation Leducq grant 22CVD01, and the American Lebanese Syrian Associated Charities (ALSAC), the fundraising and awareness organization of St. Jude.

Intrinsic Neural Dynamics Reveal a Body-Part-Specific Topography in Mouse Secondary Motor Cortex.

Recent findings suggest that the mammalian sensory cortex (S1) has a well-characterized body part-specific topography. However, most motor cortex atlases to date are only coarsely defined.

Here, we demonstrate that optical mapping of neuronal activity in awake mice reveals a distinct, body-part specific organization of mouse secondary motor cortex (M2).

Sources indicate that this M2 topography was identified by recognizing that intrinsic neuronal fluctuations are selectively synchronized between homologous sub-regions of S1 and M2. These fluctuations were strongest during rest and quenched during movement, and were not prominent in corticospinal neurons (CSNs), indicating that they do not represent motor output.

Sources indicate that functional characterization of M2 sub-regions during spontaneous movements confirms body-part specificity, and stronger engagement during multi-effector coordinated actions. Structural connectivity atlas tracings from S1 regions confirm projections to homologous M2 sub-regions.

These results reveal an crucial underlying topography within M2, and demonstrate intrinsic neuronal dynamics as a window into the functional architecture of the motor cortex.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

Recent findings suggest that “Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

Mapping the Brain’s Energy Budget: How ATP Fuels Thought

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A newly debuted study brings together 26 labs across the US and Europe to quantify the exact metabolic cost of neural computation.
  • It has been revealed that constructing a house without knowing the cost of materials, labor, or individual rooms would make architectural planning impossible.
  • To establish this foundational accounting, the Simons Foundation has launched the Simons Collaboration on Brain Energetics (SCOBE), an ambitious, decade-long international consortium uniting 26 laboratories across the United States and Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A newly debuted study brings together 26 labs across the US and Europe to quantify the exact metabolic cost of neural computation. Over a 10-year initiative, researchers will investigate how energy constraints shape brain circuits and behavior, solving mysteries such as why active brains shift toward fast, inefficient glycolysis and how glia and neuromodulators support neurons during intense cognitive demand or oxygen deprivation.

Source: Boston University / Simons Foundation.

It has been revealed that constructing a house without knowing the cost of materials, labor, or individual rooms would make architectural planning impossible. Yet for decades, neuroscientists attempting to decode how the brain processes information have operated without a quantitative metabolic blueprint. While researchers have mapped neural wiring and electrical firing patterns in exquisite detail, the exact energetic cost of thought, how much fuel the brain produces, distributes, and burns to execute specific computations, has remained largely unquantified.

To establish this foundational accounting, the Simons Foundation has launched the Simons Collaboration on Brain Energetics (SCOBE), an ambitious, decade-long international consortium uniting 26 laboratories across the United States and Europe.

Sources indicate that co-led by Dr. Anna Devor, professor of biomedical engineering at Boston University College of Engineering, and Dr. Tom Clandinin, professor of neurobiology at Stanford University, the initiative seeks to determine how strict bioenergetic limits govern neural computation from individual molecules up to whole-brain behavior.

According to recent reports, “There are lots of really cool energetics questions, but most of them are completely unanswered,” explained Dr. Devor, whose Boston University laboratory will receive $3.2 million over the next ten years as part of the program. “For example, nobody understands how the brain’s computational principles are constrained by the availability of energetic resources and how that works.”.

Every electrical impulse, synaptic release, and molecular pump in the central nervous system runs on adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the universal energy currency of living cells. Despite its fundamental role, neurobiology lacks a precise mathematical ledger detailing how much ATP different types of neural networks require to store memories, process sensory inputs, or make decisions.

“Energetics is everything,” Devor emphasized. “Our basic brain activity cannot happen unless the brain utilizes ATP, and we don’t really understand and don’t have a quantitative account of how much ATP different types of computations in the brain utilize.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of the central mysteries SCOBE investigators will tackle is a metabolic shift known as aerobic glycolysis. Under baseline resting conditions, brain cells burn glucose efficiently using oxygen inside mitochondria—the cell’s high-yield power stations. However, the moment neurons become actively engaged in a demanding cognitive task, the brain abruptly begins consuming far more sugar than can be oxidized by mitochondria, routing glucose through rapid, mitochondria-independent glycolysis.

Devor highlights two primary hypotheses driving this phenomenon:.

“These ideas are not new, but testing it experimentally requires new research tools and quantitative models. Our SCOBE consortium is perfectly positioned to deliver both,” Devor noted.

In a recent development, furthermore, the team will investigate the upstream chemical switches that turn up this metabolic dial during moments of focus and alertness. Researchers suspect that norepinephrine, a neuromodulator closely related to adrenaline that heightens arousal and cognitive acuity, directly triggers rapid glycolysis upregulation to meet sudden computational loads.

Because the brain lacks substantial internal fuel reserves, it depends on continuous vascular delivery of glucose and oxygen. Consequently, even microscopic disruptions, such as blood flow stoppages in single capillaries, can starve local neurons. Such capillary dysfunction and silent microstrokes are pervasive features of biological aging and neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer’s disease.

Paradoxically, clinical and experimental studies have also documented remarkable instances where neurons recover full cellular function following prolonged periods of oxygen deprivation, suggesting the brain possesses hidden metabolic survival mechanisms that remain poorly understood.

Unraveling these residual metabolic pathways could yield major breakthroughs in emergency medicine, guiding improved neuroprotective protocols for resuscitation following cardiac arrest or acute ischemic stroke.

Backed by the Simons Foundation’s 10-year funding horizon, double the duration of standard federal grants, and dedicated high-performance computational infrastructure to share massive neurophotonic imaging datasets across partner labs in the U.S., Norway, and Austria, SCOBE aims to build the first comprehensive energetic blueprint of the thinking brain.

What is the Simons Collaboration on Brain Energetics (SCOBE)?

Recent findings suggest that SCOBE is a 10-year international research consortium comprising 26 labs across the US and Europe, co-led by Anna Devor (Boston University) and Tom Clandinin (Stanford University). Its goal is to quantify the exact energy (ATP) costs of brain computation from the molecular level up to complex behavior.

Why does the brain switch to inefficient energy production when thinking hard?

In a recent development, during active cognitive tasks, the brain consumes extra sugar using glycolysis, a process that yields less ATP per sugar molecule than mitochondria, but operates much faster. Researchers are testing whether the brain trades efficiency for speed, or whether supportive glial cells consume this sugar to fuel active neurons.

How could mapping brain energetics improve medical treatments?

Understanding how brain cells produce energy and survive temporary oxygen shortages could lead to better treatments for stroke, microvascular aging, and neurodegenerative diseases, while improving emergency resuscitation strategies after cardiac arrest.

CRISPR Enhancer Editing Rescues Autism Brain Organoids

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers demonstrated in lab-grown human brain cells and cortical organoids that boosting the activity of a single healthy gene copy can offset the cellular effects of autism-linked genetic mutations.
  • The study used a modified CRISPR technique targeting noncoding DNA enhancers for the CHD8 and SCN2A genes, safely normalizing tissue growth and neuronal electrical firing exclusively in mutated cells without causing toxic gene overexpression.
  • Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) carries a substantial genetic component, with roughly 15% of genetic risk arising from de novo mutations, spontaneous genetic alterations that appear for the first time in a child rather than being inherited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers demonstrated in lab-grown human brain cells and cortical organoids that boosting the activity of a single healthy gene copy can offset the cellular effects of autism-linked genetic mutations.

The study used a modified CRISPR technique targeting noncoding DNA enhancers for the CHD8 and SCN2A genes, safely normalizing tissue growth and neuronal electrical firing exclusively in mutated cells without causing toxic gene overexpression.

Source: UCLA Health / Nature Neuroscience.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) carries a substantial genetic component, with roughly 15% of genetic risk arising from de novo mutations, spontaneous genetic alterations that appear for the first time in a child rather than being inherited.

Many of these high-impact mutations result in haploinsufficiency, a biological state in which one copy of a critical developmental gene is disabled, leaving the remaining healthy copy unable to produce enough protein to sustain typical neurodevelopment.

While existing clinical interventions primarily manage behavioral and cognitive symptoms, developing gene therapies to correct the underlying molecular deficits has proven exceptionally challenging, largely because delivering extra copies of large genes or directly overexpressing them can cause severe cellular toxicity.

It has been revealed that now, in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, researchers at UCLA Health led by Dr. Daniel Geschwind and Dr. George Chen have unveiled a precision epigenomic strategy that sidesteps these hurdles.

Working in human stem cell-derived neurons and three-dimensional cortical organoids, the team used a modified CRISPR system to gently turn up the volume on the body’s own remaining healthy gene copy, nudging developing brain cells back toward typical trajectories.

Rather than cutting DNA or inserting synthetic transgenes, the investigators utilized CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) directed at enhancers, specialized stretches of noncoding regulatory DNA that function like biological dimmer dials, dictating precisely when, where, and how strongly a target gene is expressed.

The team focused on two of the most prominent genes linked to autism and neurodevelopmental disorders:.

By targeting endogenous enhancers rather than the gene promoters themselves, the researchers sought to keep gene activation strictly synchronized with natural, cell-type-specific developmental rhythms and prevent dangerous overshooting into gene overexpression.

“Many autism-linked mutations leave a person with one working copy of a gene instead of two,” explained senior author Dr. Daniel Geschwind, the Gordon and Virginia MacDonald Distinguished Professor of Human Genetics, Neurology, and Psychiatry at UCLA. “Our results show that, in human cell models, it’s possible to turn up that remaining copy and move cells back toward typical development. This is a key first step, and it gives us a upcoming way to think about addressing the biology underlying these conditions.”.

To test the therapeutic potential of enhancer activation, the researchers engineered human induced pluripotent stem cells carrying CHD8 or SCN2A mutations into two advanced laboratory platforms: two-dimensional cultures of human excitatory neurons and three-dimensional cortical organoids, self-organizing clusters of brain-like tissue that recapitulate early human cortical assembly.

The results demonstrated targeted molecular and functional rescue across both genetic models:.

“What stands out to us is that the approach acted only in cell lines carrying the mutation and left healthy cell lines alone,” noted first author Dr. George Chen, a former postdoctoral fellow in the Geschwind lab and current assistant professor of neurology at Children’s Hospital of Los Angeles. “That kind of specificity matters for any future therapy. We are still a long way from the clinic, and there is a lot of work ahead on delivery and timing, but these findings provide hope and give us a clear direction.”.

The study also revealed that developmental timing plays a decisive role: enhancer activation yielded the strongest cellular rescue when applied during specific developmental windows, underscoring the dynamic nature of chromatin accessibility as neurons mature.

While the authors caution that the work represents an early-stage proof of concept conducted entirely in vitro, and that translating CRISPR enhancer therapies to patients will require overcoming major blood-brain barrier delivery hurdles and establishing efficacy beyond early embryonic windows, the implications extend far beyond CHD8 and SCN2A.

Because hundreds of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions stem from single-copy gene loss, harnessing the genome’s natural regulatory dials could provide a versatile blueprint for precision molecular medicine.

How does this upcoming CRISPR approach differ from traditional gene therapy?

Sources indicate that traditional gene therapy often attempts to replace a broken gene or permanently force it to stay switched on, which can cause toxic overexpression. Instead, the UCLA team used a modified CRISPR tool aimed at DNA “enhancers”, natural regulatory switches that control when and how strongly a gene operates, to gently boost the activity of the cell’s existing healthy gene copy within safe biological limits.

What improvements did researchers see in the lab-grown brain models?

In human cortical organoids with CHD8 mutations, boosting the healthy gene copy reduced abnormal tissue overgrowth and helped neurons mature properly. In neurons with SCN2A mutations, the approach restored normal electrical firing activity.

Why is this treatment considered promising for safety?

The CRISPR enhancer treatment only boosted gene activity in cells carrying the autism-linked mutation, leaving healthy cells and neighboring genes completely unchanged. Because it relies on existing natural gene regulation, it avoids the dangerous side effects of excessive protein production.

Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect.

We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation.

Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology.

These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

Genetic Switch Helped Evolve the Large Primate Brain

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers discovered a primate-specific DNA regulatory switch that governs the production of specialized brain-building stem cells called basal radial glia (bRG).
  • What genetic innovations enabled the human cerebral cortex, the wrinkled outer sheet of neural tissue responsible for language, abstract reasoning, perception, and memory, to grow vastly larger and more intricate than the brains of most other mammals?
  • For decades, evolutionary neurobiologists have hunted for uniquely human genes that either expand the starting pool of neural progenitor cells or prolong the developmental window during which those cells divide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers discovered a primate-specific DNA regulatory switch that governs the production of specialized brain-building stem cells called basal radial glia (bRG). The study shows that evolution expanded primate cerebral cortex complexity by altering how the shared DACH1 gene is regulated, boosting bRG progenitor production without needing to invent entirely fresh genes.

Source: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University.

What genetic innovations enabled the human cerebral cortex, the wrinkled outer sheet of neural tissue responsible for language, abstract reasoning, perception, and memory, to grow vastly larger and more intricate than the brains of most other mammals?

For decades, evolutionary neurobiologists have hunted for uniquely human genes that either expand the starting pool of neural progenitor cells or prolong the developmental window during which those cells divide.

Now, a collaborative team of researchers in Taiwan and Japan has uncovered a third evolutionary mechanism: rather than inventing newly introduced genes from scratch, evolution rewrote the regulatory instructions controlling an ancient, shared gene to alter which types of brain-building cells are manufactured.

Led by investigators at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) and Academia Sinica in Taiwan, alongside collaborators at Kyoto University in Japan, the study pinpoints a small noncoding DNA element that drives the production of basal radial glia (bRG), a specialized class of neural stem cells essential for cortical expansion.

To conceptualize how embryonic brain development evolved, the researchers compare the developing cortex to a biological factory staffed by neural stem cells. Evolution can scale up output by enlarging the workforce or extending factory operating hours, or it can modify the factory’s operating manual to produce a specialized mix of workers.

In developing primate brains, basal radial glia (bRGs) serve as high-capacity cortical builders. Abundant in humans and non-human primates yet remarkably scarce in rodents, bRGs undergo repeated rounds of self-renewing division within the outer subventricular zone, dramatically amplifying the neuronal output needed to fold and expand the cerebral cortex. They also generate upper-layer projection neurons that form long-range connections bridging distant cortical regions and hemispheres.

“What interested us was that the gene already exists in both humans and mice. The vital difference may not be the gene itself, but the instructions controlling how it is used during brain development. That gives us another way to understand how evolution could produce different kinds of brains,” explained Professor Pei-Shan Hou at the Institute of Anatomy and Cell Biology, NYCU, Taiwan.

The research team focused on DACH1 (Dachshund Family Transcription Factor 1), a developmental gene conserved across mice, monkeys, and humans. Comparative genomic analysis revealed a compact regulatory DNA sequence acting as an enhancer switch for DACH1; while conserved across primates, this regulatory motif differs in non-primate vertebrates.

To determine how this evolutionary edit shapes cortical assembly, the investigators combined cross-species stem cell engineering with live-tissue neuroimaging:.

Further molecular dissection indicated that DACH1 drives this cell-fate shift by suppressing an opposing signaling pathway that otherwise restricts neural stem cell diversification, ultimately shifting the balance of newborn neurons toward subtypes that wire the brain’s two hemispheres together.

While the authors emphasize that brain evolution and human intelligence emerge from complex, multi-gene networks rather than a single regulatory switch, the findings demonstrate how subtle tweaks in noncoding DNA can profoundly reshape cellular architecture.

By illuminating how regulatory DNA coordinates progenitor identity and developmental timing, the work provides both a clearer framework for understanding primate brain evolution and improved benchmarks for engineering high-fidelity human cortical organoids to model neurodevelopmental disorders.

How did evolution help make the human brain larger without creating new genes?

Researchers discovered that evolution modified a small regulatory stretch of noncoding DNA, acting like a genetic switch, that controls an existing gene called DACH1. By altering when and how strongly DACH1 is used during development, primates produce far more cortex-building stem cells than mice, even though both species share the DACH1 gene.

What are basal radial glia (bRG), and why are they notable?

Sources indicate that basal radial glia are specialized neural stem cells that are abundant in developing primate brains but rare in mice. They divide repeatedly to generate huge numbers of neurons for the cerebral cortex—the brain’s outer layer responsible for memory, language, and complex thought—as well as nerve cells that connect the brain’s two hemispheres.

How did scientists prove this DNA switch controls brain cell production?

In a recent development, when researchers deleted the primate regulatory DNA region from lab-grown human and rhesus monkey brain organoids, the organoids produced significantly fewer basal radial glia cells. Conversely, inserting the human DNA switch into developing mouse brains increased the production of bRG-like cells.

An LHX2-DACH1 regulatory innovation drives basal progenitor expansion in the primate neocortex.

A defining feature of the primate neocortex is an expanded cortical progenitor pool, especially the basal radial glia (bRG), contributing to complex intracortical circuitry underlying higher cognition.

Here, a comparative transcriptomic analysis of developing human and mouse neocortical cells identified DACH1 as a transcription factor enriched in human neurogenic RGs.

It has been revealed that using both primate ESCs and mouse models, we found an LHX2-DACH1-miR-215-5p program regulating bRG production. DACH1 loss in human cortical progenitors impaired bRG production and shifted neuronal output toward corticospinal neurons, whereas Dach1 depletion in mice had no effect.

Conversely, ectopic DACH1 expression in the rodent neocortex induced bRG formation and promoted callosal neuron production. Further, we found that DACH1 is regulated by LHX2 via a primate-evolved enhancer. Introducing this enhancer into mice promoted bRG generation, while its removal in primates impaired bRG production.

Recent findings suggest that mechanistically, DACH1 promotes bRG generation by suppressing miR-215-5p–mediated down-regulation of centromere- and centrosome-related genes. These findings reveal a mechanism by which cortical progenitor expansion shapes the primate cortical connectome for cognitive evolution.

Why Viruses Make You Sneeze: COVID Proteins Directly Hijack Sensory Nerves

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Neuroscientists have discovered that SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins directly activate pain-sensing nerves in the airways to trigger sneezing, coughing, and body aches, overturning the long-held view that symptoms stem solely from immune inflammation.
  • The study shows that the viral enzyme PLpro activates the wasabi-sensing TRPA1 receptor on sensory neurons, offering newly introduced therapeutic targets for acute viral symptoms and long COVID.
  • For decades, textbooks have explained the misery of respiratory infections, the racking coughs, relentless sneezing, headaches, and full-body aches, as collateral damage from the immune system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neuroscientists have discovered that SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins directly activate pain-sensing nerves in the airways to trigger sneezing, coughing, and body aches, overturning the long-held view that symptoms stem solely from immune inflammation.

The study shows that the viral enzyme PLpro activates the wasabi-sensing TRPA1 receptor on sensory neurons, offering newly introduced therapeutic targets for acute viral symptoms and long COVID.

For decades, textbooks have explained the misery of respiratory infections, the racking coughs, relentless sneezing, headaches, and full-body aches, as collateral damage from the immune system. According to conventional wisdom, infected airway cells and responding immune cells release a storm of inflammatory mediators that secondarily irritate nearby nerve endings.

Now, a study published in the journal Neuron reveals that coronaviruses do not wait for the immune system to sound the alarm; their viral proteins directly hijack the peripheral nervous system.

In a recent development, led by Dr. Diana Bautista, professor of molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley, member of the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute, and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) investigator, the research demonstrates that specific SARS-CoV-2 enzymes directly stimulate airway sensory neurons, triggering immediate sneezing, coughing, airway inflammation, and heightened pain sensitivity.

Recent findings suggest that when SARS-CoV-2 infects host cells, it manufactures two specialized enzymes, papain-like protease (PLpro) and main protease (Mpro), to slice long viral polyproteins into functional components needed for viral replication. Once the virus kills the host cell, these viral proteases spill into the surrounding airway tissue, coming into direct contact with specialized pain- and irritant-sensing neurons known as nociceptors.

Bautista, who previously discovered that the TRPA1 ion channel acts as the sensory receptor for pungent chemicals in wasabi and garlic, found that SARS-CoV-2 hijacks this exact molecular pathway:.

To test how PLpro behaves in a living organism, Bautista’s team applied just two microliters of purified PLpro to the nostrils of mice. While plain water occasionally elicited a single sneeze, PLpro triggered explosive bouts of up to 30 sneezes per minute, alongside heightened mechanical pain sensitivity.

Convincing peer reviewers that mice genuinely sneeze required rigorous physiological proof. The team acquired a specialized $75,000 plethysmograph to record the characteristic respiratory lung spasms accompanying each sneeze, matching patterns documented in other sneezing mammals, and dyed the nasal fluid blue to measure the expelled aerosol volume.

While antiviral medications like Paxlovid target Mpro to halt viral replication, numerous experimental inhibitors targeting PLpro were developed during the pandemic without yet reaching clinical approval.

“We think that these protease inhibitors that people spent a lot of time and money developing could be crucial not just for preventing viral replication,” said Bautista. “They could also help treat symptoms like coughing, which could limit viral spread, and potentially prevent severe COVID-19 in individuals who are susceptible.”.

Furthermore, direct viral sensitization of nociceptors offers a compelling biological mechanism for chronic neurological and respiratory complaints in long COVID—including persistent cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, and headaches.

“There are many modes by which viral and bacterial infections can act in our bodies — there are distinct molecular and cellular routes of triggering this type of airway hyper-reactivity,” Bautista noted. “So far, it looks like they can drive symptoms through both the immune system and the nervous system, using different molecular mechanisms.”.

How does SARS-CoV-2 cause sneezing, coughing, and body aches so rapidly?

Researchers discovered that when virus-infected cells die, they release viral enzymes, specifically papain-like protease (PLpro) and main protease (Mpro), that directly stimulate pain-sensing nerves (nociceptors) in the airways, triggering immediate sneezing, coughing, and pain rather than waiting solely for immune inflammation.

What is the TRPA1 receptor, and what does it have to do with COVID-19?

It has been revealed that TRPA1 is an ion channel on sensory nerves famously known as the “wasabi receptor” because it detects irritating chemicals in wasabi and garlic. The study found that SARS-CoV-2’s PLpro enzyme directly activates TRPA1 on airway nerves, causing the release of neuropeptides that trigger coughing, sneezing, and pain.

Could these findings lead to latest treatments for COVID-19 or long COVID?

Yes. Blocking the PLpro enzyme with targeted protease inhibitors could calm overactive sensory nerves, helping to stop severe coughing, reduce airborne viral spread, and potentially alleviate chronic neuropathic symptoms like persistent cough, chest pain, and headaches seen in long COVID.

Industry observers note that funding: The work was funded by grants from the National Institutes of Health (OD TR01 NS116992) and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Co-authors of the paper are Sonali Mali, Ricardo Silva, Zhongyan Gong, Michael Cronce, Uyen Vo, Cliff Vuong and Jeffery Cox of UC Berkeley and Yalda Moayedi of the Newly introduced York University College of Dentistry. Bautista is a member of Berkeley’s Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute.

A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain.

In a recent development, sneezing, coughing, and pain are common symptoms of respiratory viral infection. These responses are initiated by airway-innervating nociceptors that detect noxious stimuli, but how SARS-CoV-2 activates these neurons remains unclear.

Here, we show that the coronavirus papain-like protease (PLpro) directly activates airway-innervating nociceptors in mice and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived nociceptors. PLpro triggers sneezing, coughing, acute pain, and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release in the airways.

Both the proteolytic activity of PLpro and the host ion channel transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) are required for neuronal activation and sneezing. Infection with the mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 or the murine coronavirus MHV-A59 also induces sneezing in mice, and MHV-A59-evoked sneezing is TRPA1-dependent. SARS-CoV-2 infection of the trigeminal ganglia altered transcriptional programs associated with nociception, including upregulation of the TRPA1-CGRP signaling pathway activated by PLpro.

Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 triggers pain and airway reflexes and identify PLpro and TRPA1 as potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

How Lead Exposure Erodes Long-Term Memory

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, researchers uncovered the cellular mechanism by which environmental lead exposure impairs long-term memory formation.
  • Environmental lead contamination, stemming from aging lead-based paint, polluted soils, and industrial runoff, remains a pervasive global neurotoxicant, well documented to trigger learning deficits, cognitive decline, and memory impairment, particularly in developing brains.
  • Now, a research consortium in Taiwan involving Professor Ann-Shyn Chiang, President of China Medical University and Academician of Academia Sinica, alongside investigators from National Tsing Hua University, National Sun Yat-sen University, the National Health Research Institutes, and Kaohsiung Medical University, has mapped this neurotoxic pathway at cellular resolution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, researchers uncovered the cellular mechanism by which environmental lead exposure impairs long-term memory formation. The study reveals that lead disrupts oxidation-reduction balance inside neuronal mitochondria, shutting down the de novo protein synthesis needed to consolidate lasting memories, while showing that targeted antioxidants can restore memory function in fruit fly models.

Source: China Medical University.

Environmental lead contamination, stemming from aging lead-based paint, polluted soils, and industrial runoff, remains a pervasive global neurotoxicant, well documented to trigger learning deficits, cognitive decline, and memory impairment, particularly in developing brains. Yet despite decades of clinical observation, the precise molecular chain reaction through which lead disrupts memory storage inside individual neurons has remained elusive.

Now, a research consortium in Taiwan involving Professor Ann-Shyn Chiang, President of China Medical University and Academician of Academia Sinica, alongside investigators from National Tsing Hua University, National Sun Yat-sen University, the National Health Research Institutes, and Kaohsiung Medical University, has mapped this neurotoxic pathway at cellular resolution.

Published online on November 4, 2026, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), the study demonstrates that lead exposure hijacks mitochondrial redox homeostasis inside memory-consolidation neurons, starving the cell of the newly synthesized proteins required to lock short-term experiences into long-term memory.

To dissect how lead alters neural circuits without the confounding variables of mammalian systemic toxicity, the team turned to the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), a premier model organism whose memory-encoding circuits are mapped down to single identified neurons.

Behavioral assays revealed a striking dissociation:.

To observe what occurs inside the brain during memory consolidation, the researchers deployed genetically encoded redox biosensors paired with live fluorescence microscopy.

According to recent reports, the imaging pinpointed a pair of dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, cells previously established by Chiang’s group as critical hubs for translating newly synthesized proteins during long-term memory formation. Within these DAL neurons, lead exposure severely disrupted redox homeostasis, tipping mitochondrial oxidation-reduction reactions into acute oxidative stress.

Sources indicate that this mitochondrial redox imbalance directly suppressed de novo protein synthesis within the DAL neurons. Without fresh structural and synaptic proteins to remodel neural connections, newly formed memories failed to consolidate.

To verify whether mitochondrial oxidative stress was the primary driver of memory loss, and whether the deficit could be reversed, the investigators administered several antioxidant compounds to lead-exposed flies, including N-acetylcysteine (NAC), astaxanthin, resveratrol, and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), a major catechin found in green tea.

Under controlled experimental conditions, these antioxidants significantly improved long-term memory performance. Deeper cellular imaging confirmed that EGCG reduced mitochondrial oxidative imbalance and restored normal protein synthesis inside the DAL neurons. Furthermore, administering either EGCG or the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoTEMPO after a period of lead exposure restored the flies’ ability to form new long-term memories.

The authors emphasize that while these results demonstrate functional reversibility in fruit flies, they do not show the recovery of previously lost memories, nor do they establish that green tea or over-the-counter supplements can treat human lead poisoning. Further mammalian and clinical studies are necessary to determine whether targeting mitochondrial redox pathways can protect human cognition against heavy metal neurotoxicity.

How does lead exposure specifically affect memory?

In fruit fly experiments, researchers found that lead does not impair immediate learning or short-term memory. Instead, it selectively blocks the consolidation of long-term memories by preventing neurons from manufacturing the new proteins needed to stabilize those memories.

What role do mitochondria play in lead-induced memory loss?

Mitochondria regulate cellular energy and oxidation-reduction (redox) balance. Lead causes oxidative stress inside the mitochondria of memory-consolidation neurons (specifically DAL neurons), which shuts down local protein synthesis and prevents long-term memory storage.

Can antioxidants reverse memory damage caused by lead?

In the fruit fly study, antioxidants such as EGCG (found in green tea), NAC, resveratrol, and mitochondria-targeted MitoTEMPO reduced mitochondrial stress, restored neuronal protein synthesis, and allowed lead-exposed flies to form upcoming long-term memories. However, researchers caution that more studies are needed before applying these findings to humans.

Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila.

Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood.

Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila melanogaster while sparing other memory forms.

Using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation.

Antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation.

Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.

According to recent reports, latest research demonstrates that attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a systemic condition influencing respiratory patterns, subjective time pressure, brain iron levels, and alcohol use risk across the lifespan. Together, these findings reveal distinct physiological and neural signatures that extend well beyond traditional behavioral symptoms.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Affecting approximately one in nine children in the United States, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is among the most prevalent neurodevelopmental conditions of childhood. While clinical assessments have historically focused on hallmark behavioral traits, inattention, impulsivity, and motor hyperactivity, mounting evidence indicates that ADHD exerts far-reaching effects on physical and mental health well into adulthood.

Presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience, four new studies illuminate how ADHD shapes fundamental physiological and cognitive processes, ranging from involuntary breathing rhythms and subjective time perception to regional brain iron regulation and substance use vulnerability.

Taken together, the emerging findings map distinct physiological and behavioral signatures across development:.

By connecting autonomic physiology, neurochemistry, and lived cognitive stress, these studies challenge narrow definitions of ADHD as purely an attentional or behavioral disorder.

According to recent reports, “It is becoming clear that ADHD is a broader systemic condition affecting a host of brain and body variables beyond just motor hyperactivity,” remarked press conference moderator Dr. Chandan Vaidya, a cognitive neuroscientist at Georgetown University who studies how regulatory behavior goes awry in neurodevelopmental conditions. “Together, these newly introduced findings tackle timely topics and showcase the diversity of areas where work is needed to better understand ADHD and ultimately improve diagnosis and treatment.”.

How does ADHD affect physical functions outside of attention and hyperactivity?

New research presented at Neuroscience 2026 shows that ADHD is linked to distinct breathing patterns in young adults, lower iron levels in specific regions of the developing brain, and chronic psychological time pressure, demonstrating that the condition involves both brain-wide neurochemistry and bodily physiology.

What did researchers discover about brain iron in children with ADHD?

Brain scans conducted by researchers at UC San Diego revealed that children and adolescents with ADHD have lower levels of iron in specific brain regions compared to peers without ADHD. Because iron is crucial for producing neurotransmitters like dopamine, tracking these regional changes may offer latest insights into ADHD neurobiology.

Can treating ADHD help reduce alcohol misuse in young adults?

It has been revealed that yes. Emerging clinical data from the University of Florida indicates that ADHD medication may help decrease problem drinking behaviors among young adults who experience both ADHD and alcohol use disorder.

#34161. How a Video Game Helped Me Process My Grief
