What next for Shanghai? City’s art scene leans into an uncertain future

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that shanghai is a restless city.
  • According to recent reports, “Shanghai has so many galleries, so many museums, so many eccentric little spaces that you could come in the middle of summer and still see art non-stop,” says Lorenz Helbling, who founded ShanghArt in 1996.
  • The city’s two large-scale fairs, Art021 Shanghai (11-14 November) and West Bund Art & Design (10-15 November), established in 2013 and 2014 respectively, set the barometer and prime the mood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that shanghai is a restless city. Its impatient hustle may spare its art scene from the plateau of middle age as it navigates a crisis of transition after the Covid years derailed its late 2010s momentum. Going into Shanghai’s annual art week (10-15 November), with two established fairs anchoring an explosion of art events across the city, its galleries, artists and institutions are assessing how the city’s art market can weather China’s economic slowdown and whether the cultural momentum of the past three decades can be sustained.

According to recent reports, “Shanghai has so many galleries, so many museums, so many eccentric little spaces that you could come in the middle of summer and still see art non-stop,” says Lorenz Helbling, who founded ShanghArt in 1996. One of the first contemporary art galleries in China, it now has locations in Shanghai, Beijing and Singapore. The Swiss transplant says the volume of artistic activity in the city of 25 million people can be compared to Upcoming York’s, though the scene can be harder to find. “You can make a lot of fun things here.”.

The city’s two large-scale fairs, Art021 Shanghai (11-14 November) and West Bund Art & Design (10-15 November), established in 2013 and 2014 respectively, set the barometer and prime the mood. So far, Shanghai’s core galleries have largely survived China’s property crash and deflationary economy, but they need young artists and new collectors to continue buoying their businesses.

According to recent reports, lise Li, who founded Shanghai’s Vanguard Gallery in 2004, states the city is “still in an upward phase, just growing much more slowly than before”. During art week, Li’s gallery will participate in the second iteration of the boutique fair Hangover Shanghai (11-15 November) and in Art021, while showing the artist Tang Chao in the gallery and collaborating on a group show at the artist-run 33ml Offspace. Several artists represented by Vanguard are having significant moments nearby: Liao Fei will simultaneously be showing at Hangzhou’s Imagokinetics and the artist group known as Jiū Society has an exhibition at Nanjing’s Beiqiu Museum of Contemporary Art.

Established in 2013, Art021 Shanghai (pictured in 2025) is one of the most successful art fairs in the city Photo: Lisa Movius.

According to recent reports, though the buzz of the 2010s has quieted, Li claims, “there are quite a few more art institutions, and more newcomers are getting involved. The number of young artists is increasing rapidly; we see a lot of latest faces every year. But most exhibitions are relatively conservative, which is rather a pity.”.

Recent findings suggest that the market has “changed considerably” compared to what now “might be called the ‘golden 15 years’ of China’s contemporary art market: the shift in the broader economic environment over the past few years has been impossible to ignore”, Otto Neu says. In 2022 he co-founded Nan Ke Gallery, which has a group show about art and literature on view during the fair week. “For artists and galleries alike, it is certainly a challenging moment. We probably have to work twice as hard as we did before simply to survive and keep things moving.”.

Recent findings suggest that change, Neu adds, does not have to be negative. He cites the Chinese expression “great waves wash away the sand and leave the gold behind”, adding that “difficult periods can force an industry to become more focused, more rigorous and perhaps more honest about what really matters. In that sense, this may also be an crucial stage of maturation for Shanghai’s art scene.”.

In addition to this month’s two international art fairs, Shanghai’s many resident artists—ranging from established figures like Ding Yi, Zhang Enli and Yang Fudong to mid-career and emerging talents—can rely on year-round programming at a healthy variety of homegrown and imported galleries. Western outfits like Almine Rech, Perrotin and Lisson maintain spaces in Shanghai, as do Asian powerhouses including Japan’s Ota Fine Arts and Korea’s Arario Gallery. ShanghArt has been joined by several influential local galleries, among them Antenna Space, Gallery Vacancy, Capsule Gallery and Don Gallery.

Recent findings suggest that major state-backed museums like the Power Station of Art, Museum of Art Pudong and West Bund Museum (which is partnered with the Centre Pompidou in Paris) have a complement of private museums that have proliferated since the 2010s. The Rockbund Art Museum, Long Museum and Yuz Museum are the best known, but smaller, newer, specialised or further-flung institutions like Fotografiska and the Museum of Glass, and non-profit spaces like Pond Society, Longlati and Prada Rong Zhai, have also enriched the Shanghai art ecosystem.

According to recent reports, vanguard Gallery’s Li credits Shanghai’s “open-city vibe” and its large base of collectors and visitors, along with the museums, galleries and artists, plus a citizenry curious “about fashion and new things, a strong history of business, and a diverse cultural structure. The main downside is that the cost of living is too high.” The lack of art information platforms, even in Chinese, is the other main challenge, she notes.

It has been revealed that the sense of openness is what drew the collector Cherry Xu to open her art-meets-fashion space Cheruby in the city last year. With latest initiatives, “the boundaries between artists, designers, musicians and people working in fashion are becoming increasingly blurred”, she states, opening the art world to new audiences. “This kind of natural crossover between different fields is something very particular to Shanghai,” Xu says. “Art here doesn’t operate as an isolated system; it is constantly in conversation with design, music, fashion, technology and a broader youth culture, with these different communities influencing one another.”.

Sources indicate that compared to Beijing’s art scene, Neu notes, Shanghai’s creative community maintains a “healthy sense of distance. There is a certain independence between galleries, institutions, artists and collectors, which has shaped a rather distinctive ecosystem here”, a happy, pragmatic chaos of sorts. Beijing’s art scene is built on personal connections, Neu says, while in Shanghai, “between institutions, between galleries and even between galleries and collectors, there is often an understanding that business is business, friendship is friendship, and collaboration does not necessarily require complicated personal obligations or relationships”.

However, Neu adds that those divisions could become vulnerabilities in the current economic upheaval. “Perhaps this is precisely the moment when Shanghai’s art community needs to become a little more connected and cohesive than it has been in the past—not by giving up its independence, but by finding better ways to support one another,” he indicates.

Helbling states that Beijing is “more split up into scenes which work on their own”, while Shanghai has various circles that interact and are more permeable. He likens the city’s art community to its fairly compact geography, with the art neighbourhoods all within comparably easy reach of each other.

In a recent development, twenty years ago, Shanghai was the upstart artistic challenger to Beijing, the political capital home to China’s leading art academy. Hong Kong’s concurrent cultural rise proved complimentary to Shanghai’s, and many in Shanghai say the expanding art activity in Korea, Japan and Singapore—as well as in mainland Chinese cities like Chengdu, Shenzhen and nearby Nanjing, Hangzhou and Suzhou—have been net positives for the local scene.

Sources indicate that “This situation didn’t happen overnight; it’s the result of years of collaboration between Shanghai’s art institutions, galleries and fairs, as well as the collectors and artists living here,” Li claims. “It’s not simply due to fairs or art weeks alone. The rise of art in fresh Chinese cities has also become developed, likely influenced by Shanghai and Hong Kong.”.

Shanghai “was one of the earliest cities in China to develop a contemporary art market, and its relatively open culture and international outlook have given it a particular advantage”, Neu notes. “Whether we are talking about collecting, aesthetic awareness or public understanding of contemporary art, Shanghai has accumulated more than two decades of experience and audience development. That kind of cultural infrastructure takes time to build.”.

In a recent development, he adds that growing art scenes in other mainland cities represent “something very positive for Shanghai rather than a threat. A stronger regional art ecosystem ultimately creates more audiences, more conversations and more opportunities for everyone. Healthy competition and exchange between cities can only make the broader Chinese art scene more dynamic.”.

Industry observers note that regionally, Xu says, Shanghai “has a very distinct local culture, its own audiences and creative communities, [while] its relationship with other Asian cities is becoming much more direct. It feels increasingly natural for artists, curators and other creative practitioners to live and work across different cities in Asia, and for us to look to what is happening in Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok and elsewhere in the region, rather than instinctively treating Europe and the US as the only points of reference.” For Shanghai’s art week, Cheruby is showing a solo exhibition by the multidisciplinary Thai artist Tanat Teeradakorn.

“Shanghai has an interesting place within this network,” Xu notes. “It has a relatively mature art infrastructure, but also very strong fashion, design, commercial, technological and popular cultures, and these worlds exist very close to one another in everyday life. It also has a large and increasingly young audience, so when an artist comes to Shanghai, they are encountering more than an established ‘art world’; they are entering a complex and fast-moving urban environment that is constantly being reshaped by new forms of consumption, technology and youth culture. That complexity creates a lot of possibilities.”.

Zhang Ruyi, whose 2022 exhibition at Beijing’s UCCA Center for Contemporary Art is shown here, is among Shanghai’s mid-career artists to watch Photo: Sun Shi; courtesy UCCA Center for Contemporary Art.

After helping to build the careers of some of Asia’s biggest art stars, Helbling now focuses on cultivating rising talents through more group demonstrates and dialogue. “You always look at what artists are doing,” he says. “Many of them now operate between here and the West—educated here and in the West”, with networks and roots in both cultures.

Industry observers note that after suspended mobility during the Covid years, dual-culture artists in Shanghai and across Asia have resumed their frequent travels between regions. Often the children of artists or collectors, young Chinese artists are very well versed in both Western and Asian artistic traditions, giving them a sophisticated perspective. “They have an interesting job to do to figure out what kind of art makes sense today,” Helbling claims.

In a recent development, he recalls the “loneliness” of Shanghai’s 1990s avant-garde, now rendered “impossible” by contemporary art’s citywide popularity. Still, he views the 2000 internationalisation of the Shanghai Biennale, the first contemporary art fair SH Contemporary (2007-14), and the flowering of galleries and museums as all part of one era.

It has been revealed that “There was from the 1990s when Shanghai opened up until the Covid time, and there is after Covid time,” he notes. “The first 30 years, and now the second 30 years.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Learn how to build a looping Instagram Story where lines of text rotate around a 3D cube, one row at a time, using Drum wrap in ascente.design.

Reading time: about 10 minutes Â· Level: beginner-friendly Â· Format built: 1080Ã1920 MP4.

According to recent reports, kinetic typography gets a lot more interesting when the words feel like objects. In this tutorial we build a Story where four pages of text sit on the four faces of a cube, and every row of text turns on its own, one after another, like a split-flap board.

The trick is Drum wrap, a Transform setting in ascente.design that wraps a layer or a group around a cylinder or a four-sided cube. You spin it with the Tilt Y value you already know, and you animate it like any other property. No 3D software, no plugins.

What you'll need: a browser and the ascente.design editor. That's it.

Open Menu â New Design (or press âN).

In a recent development, in the dialog, choose Story (Vertical). It sets the size to 1080 Ã 1920 px. Pick the dark background and press Create document.

In a recent development, you now have a blank black artboard. Optional: select the artboard and set its fill to #000000 for pure black.

Each side of the cube is one "face", and a face is just a block of text. Press T for the Text tool, click on the artboard and type five lines, pressing Enter between them:.

Select the text layer and set these in the Design panel:.

Industry observers note that then open the Transform tab and set W = 960, X = 60 and Y = 627. A 960 px wide face leaves a 60 px margin on each side of the 1080 px artboard, and Y = 627 centers a five-line block vertically. Rename the layer Face 1 by double-clicking its name.

Sources indicate that why 960? A cube has four equal faces. Every face in this project is 960 px wide, so the whole strip will be exactly 4 Ã 960 = 3840 px.

According to recent reports, press âD to duplicate Face 1 three times. In the Transform tab, give each copy its own X position, 960 px further along each time:.

Keep Y = 627 and W = 960 on all of them. Double-click each copy on the canvas and rewrite the text. These are the pages I used:.

Industry observers note that (The extra spaces in "W R A P" spread that word out, a small nod to the original video. PERSPECTIVE is the widest word, so if it touches the edges of the face, lower the text size a little.).

The artboard hides everything outside it, so only Face 1 is visible for now. For the screenshot below I temporarily turned off the artboard's clipping to show the whole strip. The faces sit side by side, like a film strip.

It has been revealed that select all four faces in the Layers panel (the panel icon in the top bar), press âG to group them, and rename the group Cube. Check that its W is 3840.

If you slide that strip past the artboard, this is what Drum wrap is about to wrap around a cube:.

Industry observers note that select the Cube group and open the Transform tab. Scroll to Drum wrap and set:.

It has been revealed that now set the Anchor point to AX = 12.5 %. This one matters: the cube rotates around the anchor, and 12.5 % of 3840 px is 480 px, the middle of Face 1. Without it, the cube would pivot on the middle of the strip, between two faces.

Face 1 now sits flat on the front of the cube:.

Drag Tilt Y to about â40Â° and you will see two faces meeting at a corner:.

Here is Tilt Y sweeping through a full turn, so you can see every face go by:.

Quick rule: Tilt Y of 0Â° shows Face 1, â90Â° shows Face 2, â180Â° Face 3, â270Â° Face 4 and â360Â° brings you back to Face 1.

Open the motion timeline with the film icon in the top bar and set the timeline Duration to 8 s. Select the Cube group. Next to the Tilt Y field is a small diamond. Clicking it adds a keyframe at the playhead, with Easy Ease easing already applied.

Move the playhead and set Tilt Y, adding a keyframe each time:.

Because â360Â° looks exactly like 0Â°, the loop is seamless. The pairs of equal values are what make the cube pause on each face.

Recent findings suggest that right now the whole page turns as one block. To make the words feel like they are rotating one line at a time, every row becomes its own small cube.

Build one row first. Make four single-line text layers, one per face, all 960 px wide, at the same height and 960 px apart (X = 60, 1020, 1980, 2940). Group them as Row 1. Give the group the same Drum wrap settings as before: Wrap angle 360Â°, Cube, Vertical, Perspective 1700, AX = 12.5 %.

Add the same Tilt Y keyframes from Step 6 to that group.

Recent findings suggest that duplicate it. Select Row 1 and press âD. Duplicating a layer copies its keyframes too. Move each copy down by one line (140 px Ã 95 % â 133 px) and rewrite its four texts. Repeat until you have five rows, plus a small label row at the top and a page counter at the bottom if you like. My project has seven groups.

Stagger the rows. Select the keyframes on the second row's Tilt Y track and nudge them later with Alt + â, which moves them one frame at a time (add Shift for ten frames). About 7 frames at 60 fps (0.12 s) per row works well, so the third row moves 14 frames, the fourth 21, and so on. The ripple travels from top to bottom.

Because each row is its own cube, each one also gets its own vanishing point at its own height. That is what makes it read as separate bars of text, not one page.

Press the download icon in the top bar (or Menu â Export Artwork) to open the Export Studio:.

Recent findings suggest that the editor renders each frame and records it in real time, so keep the tab in front until it finishes. You'll get a standard MP4 that Instagram accepts as a Story.

Drum wrap, Tilt X / Tilt Y, Perspective and Depth Z are all per-layer settings, so everything in this tutorial works with the same controls you use elsewhere in the editor.

Recent findings suggest that want to follow along with the finished design? Open project/ascente-3d-story.ascente in ascente.design (Menu â Open).

Norfolk Coast

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Norfolk Coast is one of the UK’s best-loved and most at-risk tourist destinations.
  • We helped to define this unique destination’s strategic positioning, whilst delivering a new visual and verbal identity to promote the responsible exploration of the region, ensuring it’s here for everyone, forever.
  • Hiking, cycling and kayaking through protected landscapes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Norfolk Coast is one of the UK’s best-loved and most at-risk tourist destinations. Designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, the region is also home to Sites of Special Scientific Interest, National Nature Reserves, Marine Conservation Zones, a Biosphere Reserve and Heritage Coast. A collection of protected landscapes, united through their biodiversity and fragility. Lantern was appointed to bring these organisations together and better define and promote their common goals to preserve, restore and enhance the local life, landscapes and wildlife of the Norfolk Coast.

We helped to define this unique destination’s strategic positioning, whilst delivering a new visual and verbal identity to promote the responsible exploration of the region, ensuring it’s here for everyone, forever.

Hiking, cycling and kayaking through protected landscapes.

To fully understand what makes Norfolk so special and distinct, we embarked on a four-day immersion trip as a team. We hiked, cycled, bird watched, and conducted several interviews with local families and visitors.

It was crucial for us to discover the genuine essence of Norfolk and what it means for the local community and stakeholders who call it home, as well as identifying the key areas that require greater protection.

Norfolk’s coastal landscapes, seascapes and communities have rhythms like a heartbeat. They move across millennia, change with the seasons, and even differ day to day. Waterways widen and wander. Wildlife migrates and hibernates. Farmland flourishes and lies fallow. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. Often wild yet sometimes serene.

Our new strategy celebrates this wild, natural backdrop and all that defines it; land and sea, nature and community, they all live together in gentle harmony. And like every living thing, this delicate place deserves to be respected and protected.

Inspired by the sweeping landscapes of Norfolk’s coast and creeks we brought together the N and C of the brand name creating a unique symbol, paired with a visual language that’s full of energy and alive with nature.

Sources indicate that reflected through the interplay of type, image and illustration, we put the audience deep into the experience. To further reflect the landscape we directed an off-season photoshoot, encouraging sustainable exploration throughout the year.

It has been revealed that A suite of illustrations capture key essences from our findings and strategy along with unique wildlife and nature found in Norfolk. We utilise these within patches and stamps reflecting the positive adventures we want to encourage people to experience.

  • The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A controversy over 3m-tall erotic sculptures in northern Peru reignited recently after a senator requested that the cultural ministry remove them from a public area. Located in a park outside the city of Trujillo, the sculptures are replicas of ceramics from the pre-Incan Moche civilisation.

“What happens when children see these images? Neurological and psychological factors are affected, because they see body dimensions that are completely different from how they see themselves,” Milagros Jáuregui, a conservative senator from the Renovación Popular party, said in a speech on 26 October.

The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.

In a recent development, known as huacos eróticos, the much smaller original ceramics date from the 3rd to 8th century AD. No more than 30cm in height, they were placed in tombs as burial offerings. But the debate about their much larger versions in the park goes beyond political prudishness.

Sources indicate that “It’s a complicated matter,” the Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva tells The Art Newspaper. “There’s freedom to express or re-create themes from the past, but these ceramics were created to be placed as offerings to the dead, with a sense of revitalising life. They are associated with both fertility and an entire system of beliefs.”.

An original huaco erótico ceramic offering made by the Moche civilisation, Larco Museum, Lima Photo: László Varga, via Wikimedia Commons.

It has been revealed that the Moche civilisation covered 700km of the coast of what is now Peru, between the regions of Piura and Ancash, centuries before the Inca dominated the area. “Moche art is primarily ceramic, and these vessels depict erotic scenes or concepts of sexuality from that era,” Alva indicates. “The sculptures in the park were created outside of their historical context.”.

One of the greatest archaeological discoveries from the Moche civilisation was that of the Lord of Sipán near the city of Chiclayo—a discovery Alva made in 1987. A 3rd-century monarch, the Lord of Sipán’s body was found covered with gold along with eight other people, a dog and two llamas and nearly 500 objects including ceramic vessels, ornaments and textiles.

Industry observers note that the Moche have the largest number of erotic representations among pre-Hispanic civilisations. The most complete collection of its ceramics is in Lima, at the Larco Museum of pre-Columbian art, which celebrated its centennial in July. Before the 1960s, children were forbidden from entering the room that housed the huacos. Today, minors must be accompanied by an adult. The institution’s Erotic Gallery is one of its most popular attractions.

Jáuregui, an evangelical pastor as well as a senator, believes these Moche sculptures should only be in closed spaces. “Displaying these types of images in public is harmful to children,” she told congress. “We should have them in museums, where high-school students can observe a part of our culture that is a national treasure with the help of teachers or some kind of tutor.”.

His artistic skills include a collection of modern artworks highlighted by two unique techniques: color-changing ceramic glaze and intricate three-dimensional sculpting. In a recent development, we carefully researched and studied to include his unique artistic techniques and style in creating a new look for the museum. This involved giving the museum a new name and creating a unique custom typeface MN Vũ Thắng with “pottery-shoes-soul” inktrap touches. We wanted to echo his process and masterpieces into the content system.

Sources indicate that the brand’s visual system was created to resonate with the beauty of the various unique artworks while systematizing them into an archive through a new, clean photography style. A deliberate pottery silhouette canvas was employed for buttons and patterns across different applications, maintaining a unique and relative aesthetic. This design approach bonded to a grid system inspired by the 3-parts floor initiative layout of the museum, ensuring consistency and structure throughout the brand’s visual elements.

It has been revealed that we simplified the color palette, emphasizing the vividness and authenticity of the artwork, especially the rich colors and textures of the ceramic glaze. This focused approach highlights the authentic essence of each piece, elevating their visual impact while preserving their nature.

Collaboratively, we aimed to assemble the Bát Tràng Museum towards a more contemporary style while preserving its rich heritage.

Dynamic grids and flexible hierarchy let the same rules build a catalogue spread or a fair booth.

It runs across business cards, the binder, the pencil and the FAIRS 2026 foldout, always flat, always the same blue, never decoration.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Dubai-based art collector Elie Khouri is building a space in the city for his eponymous foundation. The Elie Khouri Art Foundation (Ekaf) will be located in the coastal district of Jumeirah 1, in a villa renovated and redesigned by Counterspace, a firm led by the architect Sumayya Vally. The space, expected to open in 2028, will host public exhibitions and educational programmes.

According to recent reports, khouri is one of the Unite Arab Emirates (UAE)’s biggest and best-known collectors. Originally from Lebanon, he made his name as the chief executive officer of Omnicom Media in the Middle East and North Africa, and has been based in Dubai since the 1990s.

He began making aims for the foundation around five years ago, as one of the London-based Deflina Foundation’s collectors-in-residence, a programme introduced in 2017 that considers collecting as a practice and seeks to support more ambitious implementation. With them he conducted feasibility studies to better understand what Dubai needs.

According to recent reports, “The whole idea is to give back and foster exchange of ideas, challenge thinking and bring upcoming perspectives,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “Dubai is about entrepreneurship. They support people like me, people coming to fulfil their ambitions. And what Dubai needs is private institutions, because that's how they will build their own version of culture.”.

Despite Dubai’s large number of artists and galleries, it has never had a major museum, and private foundations have become a significant part of its infrastructure. The Jameel Arts Centre and Alserkal Avenue, each backed by individuals, are the two pillars of the art scene, in addition to smaller foundations such as Ishara, which focuses on art from South Asia.

Ekaf has an emphasis on global contemporary art, though one in which art from the Middle East will play an notable role.

“We are here to support talent internationally,” says Khouri. “We're not about the region, but since we are in the Middle East, we also look at the best talent here. We have a responsibility to the ecosystem and the galleries.”.

Recent findings suggest that ekaf will take Khouri’s collection, comprising works by more than 300 artists, as its starting point, drawing from it for initial exhibitions. Later demonstrates will increasingly involve loans and collaborations. Ultimately, Khouri intends to establish an Ekaf collection that is separate to his personal holdings.

Industry observers note that the veteran art strategist Caroline Louca, who was formerly at Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism and Christie’s Middle East, has been appointed as the director of the foundation. Louca and Khouri are looking to hire a curatorial team closer to the completion date for the museum.

Louca underlines that community engagement will be a major part of the foundation, with prepares for talks, lectures and education streams. The foundation’s location, in Jumeirah 1, is a bonus in this respect. Jumeirah 1 is one of the oldest neighbourhoods in Dubai, where many affluent long-time residents live. Ekaf’s villa was home to an Emirati family in the 1980s, and Vally’s designs retain the elements of old-school Gulf architecture that is a source of nostalgia for many in the UAE.

"We are focusing on how we can make a place become part of the community—and not just focus on what we’re showing,” says Louca. “You can see beautiful artworks everywhere, but we want people to be a bit daring. We want them to walk in and ask questions—and not be embarrassed to ask questions—and then come back and ask more. If we can achieve that, it will be our barometer of success.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Ghanaian-French artist Kwama Frigaux and the Senegalese Fatoumata Sy have been declared as the joint winners of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize. The prize, founded by the London and Accra-based Gallery 1957 in 2021 to support women artists in Ghana and its diaspora, has this year expanded to include artists from Senegal, in partnership with Institut Français du Sénégal. Frigaux and Fatoumata have been awarded $5,000 each, as well as a three-month residency (in Senegal for the Ghanaian and in Ghana for the Senegalese), and solo exhibitions.

The prize is named after the former Ashanti queen mother, renowned for her anti-colonial resistance when Ghana was under British rule. The call for applications for this year’s edition opened in June and ran until September, and was open to Ghanaian and Senegalese women artists aged 18 or older, based either in their home countries or in the diaspora. The winners were declared during Accra Cultural Week (29 October-2 November), which is organised by Gallery 1957. On view there until 5 December is The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, a solo show by Theresah Ankomah, the winner of the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize.

Installation view of The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, Gallery 1957's show by Theresah Ankomah, who won the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Prize.

Frigaux and Sy were selected by a jury comprising Touria El Glaoui, the founder of the 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair; the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey; Marie Hélène Pereira, a senior curator at Berlin’s Haus der Kulturen der Welt; Jeanne Barral, a curator at the Fondation Cartier; the collector Alexa Waley-Cohen; and Dominique Heyse-Moore, the senior curator of contemporary British art at Tate Britain.

Runners up participate in a mentorship programme, which provides support on topics such as grant applications and entrepreneurship. Mentors this year include the Nigerian artist Modupeola Fadugba and Aisha Ayensu, the founder of the Ghanaian luxury fashion brand Christie Brown.

"I think [it's] an incredible programme that helps drive the longevity of [the prize's] impact,” Leila Zakhem, the director of the prize, tells The Art Newspaper. “And it really creates a beautiful community.”.

Recent findings suggest that zakhem explains that her team considered several countries for the expansion, including Nigeria. A key part of this search was finding a "very good implementing partner". The Institut Français du Sénégal, which is a non-commercial space, has a lot of credibility, she adds, “and they were very excited to partner with us on the prize”. Zakhem says that she hopes the expansion will help develop and create a bridge between art communities in English- and French-speaking West Africa.

Industry observers note that the planned next steps are to expand further into West Africa, and then potentially beyond, with winners selected from different regions of the continent. “The goal is eventually to be the leading Pan-African female art prize on the continent,” Zakhem says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The key to belonging may be more within your reach than you think. You don’t need to become more interesting, more confident, or less awkward. You may simply need to become more psychologically flexible.

Psychological flexibility is your capacity to stay present, open to your inner experience, and engaged with what matters to you—even when things feel uncomfortable. Researchers have been studying this capacity for decades, and it turns out that when you are more psychologically flexible, you are not only less likely to struggle with anxiety and depression, you are also more capable of pursuing what matters to you. That might mean repairing  strained relationships, joining the exercise class you feel anxious about, or starting the book club you know would bring more conversation and connection into your life.

Our sense of belonging may be shaped, at least in part, by how we respond to the difficult thoughts and feelings that arise when we reach for connection.

It has been revealed that A recent study of more than 16,000 undergraduate students at 104 U.S. colleges and universities found that greater psychological flexibility was associated with a stronger sense of belonging. The study does not prove that flexibility causes belonging, but it points to something hopeful: Our sense of belonging may be shaped, at least in part, by how we respond to the difficult thoughts and feelings that arise when we reach for connection.

Emotional flexibility is your capacity to make room for the range of feelings that can come with being part of a group—whether you’re feeling left out, awkward, or nervous—without becoming overwhelmed by those emotions or needing to suppress them.

Meeting new people can feel awkward, getting past small talk can be tedious, and encountering people with different views can sometimes be irritating.

In a recent development, sometimes our emotions give us important information. Maybe you are dreading that work event because there’s heavy drinking, and it doesn’t align with your values. That discomfort may be worth listening to. At other times, feeling uncomfortable is simply part of the experience. Meeting new people can feel awkward, getting past small talk can be tedious, and encountering people with different views can sometimes be irritating.

Try this small emotional flexibility practice: Imagine placing the feelings you’re having about a social situation into a backpack. How do you want to carry them? Do you want to shift the weight from side to side? Find someone to help you carry it? Or perhaps offer yourself some self compassion along the way? You may not get to decide what is inside the backpack, but you can decide how you carry it into your next interaction.

Recent findings suggest that every so often, look inside. Do these feelings have useful information for you? Do they  need care or attention? If not, adjust the straps and bring them along.

According to recent reports, your mind can be the world’s worst co-pilot when it comes to social situations. It compares you to others, judges you, makes negative predictions and sometimes is just plain mean.

Cognitive defusion is the practice of stepping back from our thoughts rather than automatically treating them as facts.

In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), cognitive defusion is the practice of stepping back from our thoughts rather than automatically treating them as facts.

According to recent reports, before entering a social event, write down some of the thoughts you’re having. Just noting a thought is a thought, helps you get some space from it. You get to decide if you want to take your mind’s advice, or just say thank you and move on.

According to recent reports, try this  cognitive defusion practice: When unhelpful thoughts return, try responding: “Thank you, mind. I know you are trying to help me. And I’ve decided to do this.”.

The goal is not to get rid of the thoughts. It is to stop allowing them to make all your social decisions.

Sources indicate that when we feel as though we don’t belong, we often see ourselves through a narrow lens: I am not good at conversation. I am the only person who doesn’t know someone here. I never make a good first impression.

You know you are limiting yourself when you use phrases like: I am, I always, I never, I am the only one who….

You know you are limiting yourself when you use phrases like:.

I am, I always, I never, I am the only one who….

According to recent reports, these kinds of statements can make a passing experience feel like a permanent part of who we are. But pretty much everyone has felt socially awkward at one time or another, and nearly everyone longs to belong. And chances are, you aren’t always this way.

Try this self-flexibility practice: When you notice a  narrow view of yourself taking over, see whether you can become more flexible with your idea of “me.” Can you notice someone else who may be feeling similarly? Can you recognize a way that you are already connected—through your nervousness, or simply by sharing this moment? And can you see yourself as someone who isn’t defined by  “always” and “never”? What changes when you make room for sometimes instead?

Industry observers note that in ACT, values describe how you want to show up in your life. They are qualities of action— such as courageously, warmly, playfully, honestly, or presently.

Recent findings suggest that before entering a social situation, try this values practice. Ask yourself:.

How do I want to make others feel?

If I already felt like I fit in, how would I act?

According to recent reports, these questions help you identify how you want to participate and connect with others. You don’t have to wait until you feel confident or included. In fact, the more you act in alignment with your values, the more you may begin to experience yourself as someone who already belongs.

Recent findings suggest that social anxiety has a way of pulling our attention inward. It shines a spotlight on how we look, whether we’re stumbling over our words, or what might go wrong next.

According to recent reports, try being more flexible with your attention. Notice your feet on the floor, listen to what the other person has to say, or take in the group as a whole. Shifting your focus like this can help you become less caught up in self-consciousness and more aware of what’s happening around you. There’s more to the scene than the words you are saying.

Try this attentional flexibility practice: When you notice yourself getting caught up in comparison or self-judgment, try shifting your attention. What are five things you see? What are four things you hear? What are three things you care about? What are two people you want to meet? What is one thing that matters most to you right now?

When you feel the longing to belong, try acting on it in a small way.

We build belonging one small connection at a time.

In a recent development, when you feel the longing to belong, try acting on it in a small way. At the grocery store, strike up a conversation with the person grabbing lettuce next to you (“What salad are you making?”) At school pickup, get out of your car and wait with other caregivers (“Who’s your kid?”). If you are waiting for a yoga class to start, talk to the person next to you (“Have taken this class before?”) If  someone is sharing the space with you, you already have something in common. It takes courage to make that move, but small gestures like these can open the door to meaningful connections over time.

Industry observers note that use your other psychological flexibility skills to support you! Make room for discomfort, step back from unhelpful thoughts, shift your attention away from self-judgement, broaden your perspective,  and remember why you want to connect in the first place.

According to recent reports, psychological flexibility offers you a greater range of ways to respond, even when you feel like you don’t quite fit in. You can make room for anxiety, step back from your mind’s commentary, widen your sense of self, orient toward your values, return to the present, and make one small move toward connection.

Try out some of these skills, and you will notice, belonging is something you co-create, one flexible move at a time.

Diana Hill, PhD is a clinical psychologist, international trainer and sought-out speaker on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and compassion. Host of the Wise Effort podcast, author of The Self-Compassion Daily Journal, and co-author the ACT Daily Journal. @drdianahill.
